about: ELEC40009 is a 7.5 ECTS first-year Electrical and Electronic Engineering module at Imperial that shows how three areas of electrical engineering connect: semiconductor devices (autumn term: carriers and energy bands, the pn diode and solar cell, BJT and MOSFET), electrical power (supply systems, solar energy, PV interfaces, switch-mode supplies and changing grids) and communications (signals, frequency content and convolution, AM and FM, and, if time permits, a brief introduction to digital communications). It is taught through lectures, problem classes and regular quizzes. According to the module descriptor (last revised January 2025), it is assessed by three timed, invigilated, computer-based exams: semiconductor devices (34%, start of spring term), power electronics (33%, spring mid-term period) and communications (33%, summer exam period).
topics: Electrical supply systems and solar energy

notes.body:
The devices part of the module starts with how charge moves in silicon. Everything later (diodes, solar cells, transistors) depends on these ideas.

Energy bands
- In a crystal, the allowed electron energies form bands. The valence band is (nearly) full; the conduction band above it is (nearly) empty. Between them is the band gap E_g.
- Silicon has E_g ≈ 1.12 eV at room temperature. Insulators have large gaps; metals have overlapping or partly filled bands.
- An electron excited into the conduction band is free to move. The empty state it leaves in the valence band behaves as a positive carrier, the hole.
- A photon can create an electron–hole pair only if its energy hf exceeds E_g. For silicon this means wavelengths below about 1240/1.12 ≈ 1100 nm, which is why silicon solar cells use visible and near-infrared light.

Intrinsic and doped silicon
- In pure (intrinsic) silicon, electron and hole concentrations are equal: n = p = n_i, about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K. The modern accepted value is about 9.65 × 10⁹ cm⁻³; older textbooks quote 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, so use whatever value the question gives.
- n-type: add donors from group V (phosphorus, arsenic). Each gives an electron, so n ≈ N_D.
- p-type: add acceptors from group III (boron). Each accepts an electron, creating a hole, so p ≈ N_A.
- Mass-action law in equilibrium: np = n_i². So in n-type silicon with N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, the hole (minority carrier) concentration is p = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³.
- Majority carriers dominate conduction; minority carriers matter for diodes, BJTs and solar cells.

The Fermi level
- E_F marks the energy at which the probability of occupation is one half.
- Intrinsic: E_F near mid-gap. n-type: E_F moves towards the conduction band. p-type: E_F moves towards the valence band.
- In equilibrium, E_F is flat across any junction. This is what produces band bending in a pn junction.

Carrier transport
- Drift: carriers accelerate in an electric field E; drift velocity v = μE, where μ is the mobility (electrons are more mobile than holes in silicon).
- Conductivity σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p); resistivity ρ = 1/σ.
- Example: N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³, μ_n = 1350 cm²/V s gives σ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1350 ≈ 2.16 S/cm, so ρ ≈ 0.46 Ω cm.
- Diffusion: carriers move from high to low concentration; current density proportional to the concentration gradient, with diffusion coefficient D.
- Einstein relation D/μ = kT/q = V_T ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K.
- Generation and recombination: pairs are created thermally or optically and recombine after a lifetime τ.

Exam tips: state which carrier is the majority, always use np = n_i² for the minority concentration, and keep units in cm⁻³ and cm²/V s consistently.

notes.h: The pn diode and the solar cell
notes.body:
Joining p-type and n-type silicon creates the pn junction, the basis of diodes, solar cells and (twice over) the BJT. The descriptor's reading list (January 2025) points to chapter 5 of Streetman and Banerjee, Solid State Electronic Devices.

Forming the junction
- Electrons diffuse from the n side to the p side and holes the other way, leaving behind fixed ionised donors (+) and acceptors (−). This is the depletion (space-charge) region.
- The fixed charge sets up an electric field that opposes further diffusion. In equilibrium, drift and diffusion currents balance for each carrier.
- Built-in potential V_bi = V_T ln(N_A N_D/n_i²). For N_A = N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ this is about 0.71 V.
- On a band diagram the bands bend by qV_bi while the Fermi level stays flat.

Biasing
- Forward bias (p positive) lowers the barrier, and minority carriers are injected across the junction, giving a current that rises exponentially with voltage.
- Reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the depletion region; only a small saturation current flows, made of thermally generated minority carriers. Large reverse voltages cause breakdown (avalanche or Zener).
- Ideal diode equation: I = I_S (e^(V/V_T) − 1). At 300 K the current rises tenfold for every V_T ln 10 ≈ 60 mV of extra forward bias.

Equivalent-circuit components from physics
- Small-signal (incremental) resistance r_d = V_T/I_D, the slope of the exponential.
- Junction (depletion) capacitance: the depletion region acts like a parallel-plate capacitor whose width changes with bias, so the capacitance falls under reverse bias.
- Diffusion capacitance: stored minority charge in forward bias, proportional to the current.

The solar cell
- Light with photon energy above E_g creates electron–hole pairs. Pairs generated in or near the depletion region are swept apart by the junction field, giving a photocurrent I_L that flows in the reverse direction.
- Taking generated current as positive: I = I_L − I_S(e^(V/V_T) − 1).
- Short-circuit current I_sc ≈ I_L (proportional to irradiance).
- Open-circuit voltage V_oc = V_T ln(I_L/I_S + 1). It grows only logarithmically with light: halving I_L lowers V_oc by V_T ln 2 ≈ 18 mV.
- Example: I_L = 3 A, I_S = 10⁻¹⁰ A gives V_oc ≈ 0.025 85 × ln(3 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 0.62 V.
- Maximum power point (MPP): the point on the I–V curve where V·I is greatest.
- Fill factor FF = P_max/(V_oc I_sc), typically 0.7 to 0.85 for good silicon cells.
- Efficiency = P_max/(irradiance × area).
- Equivalent circuit: current source I_L in parallel with a diode, plus a series resistance (contacts, bulk) and a shunt resistance (leakage paths). Series resistance lowers the fill factor at high current.
- Heating lowers V_oc, so cells produce less power when hot.

Exam tips: be ready to sketch both the dark and illuminated I–V curves, mark I_sc, V_oc and the MPP, and explain each element of the equivalent circuit physically.

The module derives the output and control characteristics of the two main transistors from carrier transport. Focus on the physical story and on the equations that come out of it.

Bipolar junction transistor (npn)
- Three regions: heavily doped n⁺ emitter, thin lightly doped p base, n collector.
- Active mode: base–emitter junction forward biased, base–collector junction reverse biased.
- The forward-biased emitter junction injects electrons into the base. The base is much thinner than the electrons' diffusion length, so nearly all of them diffuse across and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased collector junction's field.
- A small base current supplies holes lost to recombination in the base and holes injected back into the emitter. Heavy emitter doping keeps that back-injection small.
- Control characteristic: I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T): the collector current is set exponentially by V_BE.
- α = I_C/I_E (just below 1) and β = I_C/I_B = α/(1 − α). β = 100 gives α ≈ 0.990.
- Output characteristic: in active mode I_C is nearly independent of V_CE. The Early effect (base-width modulation) gives a slight upward slope, modelled by the Early voltage V_A.
- Other regions: saturation (both junctions forward biased, V_CE ≈ 0.2 V) and cut-off.

MOSFET (n-channel enhancement)
- A metal (or polysilicon) gate over a thin oxide on p-type silicon, with n⁺ source and drain.
- A positive gate voltage repels holes and attracts electrons. Above the threshold voltage V_t, an inversion layer (n channel) forms at the surface and links source and drain.
- The gate oxide is an insulator, so the gate draws no DC current; the gate and channel form a capacitor with capacitance per unit area C_ox.
- Channel charge per unit area ≈ C_ox(V_GS − V_t − V(x)), and drift along the channel gives the current.
- Triode region (V_DS < V_GS − V_t): I_D = μ_nC_ox(W/L)[(V_GS − V_t)V_DS − ½V_DS²]. For small V_DS it is a voltage-controlled resistor.
- Saturation (V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_t): the channel pinches off at the drain end and I_D = ½μ_nC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_t)², the square law.
- Doubling the overdrive V_GS − V_t therefore quadruples the saturation current.
- Example: μ_nC_ox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 10, V_t = 0.5 V, V_GS = 1.0 V gives I_D(sat) = ½ × 2 mA/V² × 0.25 V² = 250 μA for V_DS ≥ 0.5 V.

Comparing the two
- BJT: exponential control law, higher transconductance for a given current, finite base current.
- MOSFET: square-law control, essentially zero gate current, easy to make small, dominant in digital CMOS.

Exam tips: be ready to sketch a family of output curves (I_C against V_CE for several I_B, or I_D against V_DS for several V_GS), label the regions and the boundary V_DS = V_GS − V_t, and explain each region physically.

notes.h: Electrical supply systems and solar energy
notes.body:
The power section of the module starts with how a national electricity system is arranged and where solar energy fits.

Why AC and three-phase
- AC lets transformers change voltage easily and efficiently, so power can be generated at one voltage, transmitted at a much higher one and used at a low one.
- Three-phase systems carry three sinusoids 120° apart. For balanced loads the total instantaneous power is constant, and three wires (plus neutral) carry three times the power of one single-phase pair with less conductor material per watt.
- Line (phase-to-phase) voltage = √3 × phase (phase-to-neutral) voltage in a star connection. The UK low-voltage supply is 230 V phase, 400 V line, at 50 Hz.

Why high voltage for transmission
- For a given power P = VI (unity power factor), current I = P/V, and the line loss is I²R = P²R/V².
- Losses therefore fall with the square of voltage: carrying the same power at 400 kV instead of 132 kV cuts the losses by (400/132)² ≈ 9.2 times.

Structure of the GB system
- Generation: large power stations (gas, nuclear, biomass), wind farms, solar farms and interconnectors.
- Transmission: 400 kV and 275 kV (and 132 kV in Scotland), a meshed national network.
- Distribution: 132 kV (in England and Wales), 33 kV and 11 kV down to 400/230 V for homes. Distribution networks were traditionally radial, with power flowing one way.
- Frequency is common across the synchronous system (50 Hz) and must be held close to nominal by matching generation to demand second by second.

Solar energy basics
- Irradiance is power per unit area (W/m²). Standard test conditions (STC) use 1000 W/m², a cell temperature of 25 °C and a standard spectrum (AM1.5).
- Panel power at STC = irradiance × area × efficiency. A 1.7 m² panel at 20 % efficiency gives 1000 × 1.7 × 0.2 = 340 W, quoted as 340 Wp (watts peak).
- Real output varies with time of day, season, cloud, orientation and tilt, shading and temperature (hotter cells give less power).
- Energy yield is often expressed per kWp installed per year; multiply by system size to estimate annual energy.
- Capacity factor = actual energy produced/(rated power × hours). Solar capacity factors are much lower than those of thermal plant because of night and weather.

Solar in the grid
- Large solar farms connect at distribution or transmission voltage; rooftop PV connects at 230/400 V.
- PV produces DC, so power electronics (the next topic) is needed to connect it to the AC network.
- Output is variable and partly predictable, so it must be balanced by other generation, storage or demand response.

Exam tips: show the I²R loss argument with an explicit ratio, distinguish phase and line voltages, and always state the irradiance and efficiency assumptions in solar calculations.

notes.h: Photovoltaic interfaces and switch-mode power supplies
notes.body:
A PV panel gives a DC voltage and current that vary with sunlight; the grid wants 50 Hz AC at a fixed voltage. Switch-mode power electronics makes the connection efficiently.

Why switch-mode?
- A linear regulator drops the excess voltage across a transistor and turns it into heat, so its efficiency is roughly V_out/V_in.
- A switch-mode converter turns a transistor fully on and fully off at high frequency (tens of kHz and above). An ideal switch has either zero voltage or zero current, so it dissipates no power, and an inductor and capacitor store and release energy to set the average output. Efficiencies above 95 % are common.
- Duty cycle D = t_on/T, the fraction of each period the switch is on.

Basic DC–DC converters (ideal, continuous conduction, steady state)
- The key rule: in steady state the average inductor voltage over a period is zero (volt–second balance).
- Buck (step-down): V_out = D V_in. Example: 48 V to 12 V needs D = 0.25.
- Boost (step-up): V_out = V_in/(1 − D). Example: 30 V to 400 V needs D = 1 − 30/400 = 0.925.
- Buck–boost (inverting): V_out = −D V_in/(1 − D).
- Ideal converters conserve power: V_in I_in = V_out I_out, so a buck converter steps current up as it steps voltage down.
- Buck inductor ripple: ΔI_L = (V_in − V_out) D/(f L). Higher switching frequency or larger L means less ripple.

The PV interface chain
- PV array (DC, voltage depends on light and temperature).
- DC–DC stage, often a boost, which raises the voltage to a DC link and performs maximum power point tracking (MPPT).
- DC link capacitor to buffer energy.
- Inverter: a bridge of switches driven by pulse-width modulation (PWM) synthesises a sinusoidal voltage. A filter (inductor, sometimes LCL) removes the switching ripple.
- Grid connection, sometimes through a transformer for isolation. The inverter synchronises to the grid (typically using a phase-locked loop) and injects current in phase with the voltage.
- Protection: the inverter must disconnect if the grid fails (anti-islanding).

Maximum power point tracking
- The PV I–V curve has a single maximum power point that moves with irradiance and temperature.
- MPPT adjusts the converter's duty cycle (and so the panel's operating voltage) to stay at that point.
- Perturb and observe: nudge the voltage, measure the power; keep going if the power rose, reverse if it fell.

Exam tips: derive conversion ratios from volt–second balance rather than memorising them, check that D lies between 0 and 1, and use power conservation to find currents on the other side of a converter.

The final power topic asks how electricity systems must change as net-zero targets are pursued. Expect discussion questions that need specific, well-explained mechanisms rather than slogans.

From the traditional grid
- Large synchronous generators (coal, gas, nuclear) at transmission level, power flowing one way down to consumers, and output adjusted to follow a fairly predictable demand.
- Britain's last coal-fired power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed on 30 September 2024; wind and solar now supply a large and growing share.

Key challenges
- Variability and uncertainty: wind and solar output depend on weather and time of day. Supply must still match demand every second, so the system needs flexibility.
- Inertia: synchronous machines store kinetic energy in their rotating masses. When a generator trips, that energy is released automatically and slows the fall in frequency. Wind and solar connect through inverters and provide no inherent inertia, so frequency can fall faster.
- Rate of change of frequency (RoCoF): from the swing equation, initial RoCoF ≈ ΔP f₀/(2E_k), where E_k is the stored kinetic energy. Losing 1 GW with E_k = 100 GW s at 50 Hz gives about 0.25 Hz/s, and the frequency falls.
- System strength and fault current: inverters supply limited fault current, which affects protection and voltage stability.
- Distribution networks: rooftop PV, heat pumps and electric vehicles change local power flows. At midday PV can exceed local demand and power flows back up the network (reverse power flow), raising local voltages towards their limits.
- Network capacity: new generation is often far from demand (for example offshore wind), requiring new transmission and long connection queues.
- Electrification of heat and transport increases peak demand.

Solutions
- Storage: batteries (fast frequency response, daily shifting), pumped hydro, longer-duration options.
- Demand-side response and smart charging: shifting flexible loads to times of high renewable output.
- Interconnectors to neighbouring systems.
- Grid-forming inverters that set voltage and frequency themselves and can emulate inertia; synchronous condensers that add inertia and fault current without generating.
- Smarter distribution: active network management, on-load tap changers, curtailment when needed.
- Better forecasting and markets that reward flexibility.

Writing good answers
- Name the physical mechanism (energy balance, inertia, voltage rise from reverse flow).
- Link each problem to a specific solution and its limitation (batteries respond in milliseconds but have limited energy).
- Use numbers where you can.

Exam tips: structure discussion answers as problem, mechanism, solution, trade-off, and use the RoCoF formula to show why low inertia matters.

The communications section relies on Fourier analysis. Lathi and Ding's Modern Digital and Analog Communication Systems is on the descriptor's reading list (January 2025).

Classifying signals
- Continuous-time vs discrete-time; analogue (any amplitude) vs digital (a finite set of levels).
- Periodic (x(t + T₀) = x(t) for all t) vs aperiodic.
- Deterministic (fully described by a formula) vs random (described statistically, like noise or a speech signal).
- Energy signals have finite energy E = ∫|x(t)|² dt (for example a single pulse); power signals have finite, non-zero average power (for example a sinusoid, power A²/2).

Time and frequency domains
- Any periodic signal can be written as a Fourier series: a sum of sinusoids at the fundamental f₀ = 1/T₀ and its harmonics nf₀.
- A square wave of amplitude ±A contains only odd harmonics, with amplitudes 4A/(nπ): falling as 1/n. A triangle wave also has only odd harmonics, but they fall as 1/n², so it looks smoother.
- Aperiodic signals have a continuous spectrum given by the Fourier transform X(f) = ∫x(t)e^(−j2πft) dt.
- Rectangular pulse of height A and width T ↔ AT·sin(πfT)/(πfT): a sinc-shaped spectrum with its first zero at f = 1/T. Shorter pulses have wider spectra; this time–bandwidth trade-off is central to communications.
- Real signals have spectra with even magnitude, so we often draw only positive frequencies.

Useful Fourier properties
- Time shift: a delay multiplies the spectrum by a linear phase e^(−j2πft₀) but leaves the magnitude unchanged.
- Frequency shift (modulation): multiplying x(t) by cos(2πf_c t) moves half the spectrum up to +f_c and half down to −f_c. This is the basis of AM.
- Time scaling: compressing a signal in time stretches its spectrum.

Convolution
- y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = ∫x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ: the output of a linear time-invariant system with impulse response h(t).
- Graphically: flip one signal, slide it across the other and integrate the overlap at each shift.
- Convolving two equal rectangular pulses of width T gives a triangle of width 2T.
- Convolution in time ↔ multiplication in frequency: Y(f) = X(f)H(f). So a filter shapes a spectrum by multiplying it.
- Multiplication in time ↔ convolution in frequency.

Bandwidth
- The range of positive frequencies a signal occupies (or a system passes). Speech for telephony is about 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz; high-quality audio extends to about 15 to 20 kHz.

Exam tips: sketch both time and frequency pictures for every signal, and remember the two dualities: narrow in time means wide in frequency, and convolution in one domain is multiplication in the other.

Modulation shifts a message signal m(t) (bandwidth W) up to a carrier frequency f_c so that it can be radiated by a practical antenna and so that many signals can share the spectrum.

Double-sideband suppressed carrier (DSB-SC)
- s(t) = m(t) cos(2πf_c t). By the frequency-shift property the spectrum is M(f) copied to ±f_c, with upper and lower sidebands.
- Bandwidth 2W.
- Demodulation needs a local carrier of the same frequency and phase (coherent detection): multiply by cos(2πf_c t) again and low-pass filter.

Conventional AM (DSB with carrier)
- s(t) = [A + m(t)] cos(2πf_c t). Modulation index μ = m_p/A, where m_p is the peak magnitude of m(t).
- For a single tone, s(t) = A[1 + μ cos(2πf_m t)] cos(2πf_c t), giving a carrier at f_c and two sidebands at f_c ± f_m, each of amplitude μA/2.
- If μ ≤ 1 the envelope A + m(t) never goes negative, so a simple envelope detector (diode, resistor, capacitor) recovers m(t). If μ > 1 (overmodulation) the envelope distorts.
- Bandwidth 2W, the same as DSB-SC.
- Power for tone modulation: P_total = P_c(1 + μ²/2). Power efficiency η = μ²/(2 + μ²), at most 1/3 at μ = 1. Most power sits in the carrier, which carries no information. That is the price of a cheap receiver.
- Single sideband (SSB) transmits one sideband only, halving bandwidth to W.

Frequency modulation (FM)
- The instantaneous frequency varies with the message: f_i(t) = f_c + k_f m(t).
- Peak frequency deviation Δf = k_f m_p. Deviation ratio (modulation index for a tone) β = Δf/W.
- The amplitude is constant, so FM is robust to amplitude noise and works with efficient non-linear power amplifiers.
- Carson's rule estimates bandwidth: B ≈ 2(Δf + W).
- Example: broadcast FM with Δf = 75 kHz and W = 15 kHz needs about 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz.
- Narrowband FM (β ≪ 1) occupies about 2W, like AM. Wideband FM trades extra bandwidth for better output signal-to-noise ratio.
- Demodulation: a frequency discriminator (for example differentiate, then envelope-detect) or a phase-locked loop.

Phase modulation (PM)
- Phase varies with m(t). PM and FM are closely related: FM is PM of the integral of the message.

Comparing AM and FM
- AM: narrow bandwidth, simple receiver, poor power efficiency, sensitive to amplitude noise.
- FM: wider bandwidth, better noise performance, constant envelope.

Exam tips: sketch spectra with frequencies and amplitudes labelled, state Carson's rule explicitly, and check μ ≤ 1 before proposing an envelope detector.

The descriptor lists a brief introduction to digital communications "if time permits", so this topic may be lighter in your year. The core ideas are sampling, quantisation and digital modulation.

Sampling
- Sampling theorem: a signal band-limited to B Hz can be reconstructed exactly from samples taken at f_s ≥ 2B (the Nyquist rate).
- Sampling in time makes the spectrum repeat around multiples of f_s. If f_s < 2B the copies overlap: aliasing, where high frequencies masquerade as low ones and cannot be removed afterwards.
- An anti-aliasing low-pass filter before the sampler limits the bandwidth. In practice f_s is set a little above 2B to leave room for real filters (telephone speech, limited to about 3.4 kHz, is sampled at 8 kHz).

Quantisation and PCM
- Each sample is rounded to one of L = 2ⁿ levels and coded as n bits: pulse code modulation (PCM).
- Bit rate R_b = n f_s. Telephone PCM: 8 bits × 8000 samples/s = 64 kbit/s.
- Quantisation introduces an error of up to half a step. For a full-scale sinusoid the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio is about 6.02n + 1.76 dB: each extra bit gives about 6 dB.

Why go digital?
- Regeneration: repeaters can decide which symbol was sent and re-create a clean signal, so noise does not accumulate over distance.
- Error-control coding can detect and correct errors.
- Easy encryption, compression and multiplexing of many sources.
- The cost is bandwidth: PCM needs much more than the original analogue signal.

Baseband transmission
- Line codes represent bits as pulses (for example polar NRZ: +V for 1, −V for 0).
- The minimum bandwidth needed to send R symbols per second without intersymbol interference is R/2 (Nyquist).

Digital modulation (bandpass)
- Amplitude-shift keying (ASK): the carrier amplitude switches (on–off keying is the simplest).
- Frequency-shift keying (FSK): different frequencies for 0 and 1.
- Phase-shift keying (PSK): BPSK uses phases 0 and π; QPSK uses four phases and carries 2 bits per symbol.
- M-ary schemes carry log₂M bits per symbol, saving bandwidth at the cost of needing a higher signal-to-noise ratio.
- These are the digital counterparts of AM, FM and PM.

Channel capacity
- Shannon: C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bit/s is the upper limit for error-free transmission over a channel of bandwidth B with Gaussian noise.

Exam tips: always check the sampling rate against 2B, show the bit-rate calculation, and link each digital scheme to its analogue counterpart.

cards.b: About 1.12 eV at room temperature; photons need hf > E_g (λ below about 1100 nm) to create electron–hole pairs.
The vacant state left in the valence band when an electron is excited; it behaves as a mobile positive charge carrier.
In equilibrium np = n_i², so the minority concentration is n_i² divided by the majority concentration.

cards.f: Donor and acceptor dopants in silicon
cards.b: Donors are group V (P, As) giving n-type; acceptors are group III (B) giving p-type.

cards.f: Fermi level position in n-type silicon
cards.b: Above mid-gap, closer to the conduction band; in p-type it is closer to the valence band.
σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p); for doped material the majority term dominates.
D/μ = kT/q = V_T, linking diffusion coefficient and mobility (≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K).
Drift is driven by an electric field (v = μE); diffusion by a concentration gradient.
Region near the junction emptied of mobile carriers, leaving fixed ionised dopants whose field opposes diffusion.
V_bi = V_T ln(N_A N_D/n_i²); about 0.7 V for typical silicon doping.
I = I_S(e^(V/V_T) − 1); current rises about tenfold per 60 mV at 300 K.
r_d = V_T/I_D, the inverse slope of the I–V curve at the bias point.
V_oc = V_T ln(I_L/I_S + 1); it increases only logarithmically with light intensity.
FF = P_max/(V_oc I_sc); a measure of how 'square' the I–V curve is.

cards.f: Series and shunt resistance in a solar cell
cards.b: Series R (contacts, bulk) and low shunt R (leakage) both reduce the fill factor and output power.
Junction: depletion charge, dominant in reverse bias. Diffusion: stored minority charge, proportional to forward current.

cards.f: Why the BJT base is thin
cards.b: So that injected carriers cross it by diffusion before recombining, making α close to 1 and β large.
β = α/(1 − α) and α = β/(β + 1); β = 100 gives α ≈ 0.990.
I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T) in active mode: an exponential dependence on base–emitter voltage.
Base-width modulation by V_CE makes I_C rise slightly with V_CE; modelled by the Early voltage V_A.
The gate–source voltage at which a conducting inversion layer forms under the gate.
At V_DS = V_GS − V_t the channel vanishes at the drain end; beyond this the current saturates.
I_D = ½μ_nC_ox(W/L)(V_GS − V_t)²: a square law in the overdrive voltage.
For fixed power, I = P/V, so I²R losses fall as 1/V²; transformers make voltage changes easy with AC.
V_line = √3 × V_phase; UK LV supply is 230 V phase, 400 V line.
400 kV and 275 kV (plus 132 kV in Scotland).
50 Hz, common across the synchronous network and held by balancing generation and demand.
1000 W/m² irradiance, 25 °C cell temperature, AM1.5 spectrum; used for a panel's peak (Wp) rating.
Actual energy delivered divided by (rated power × time); low for solar because of night and weather.
Higher cell temperature lowers V_oc and hence power output.
D = t_on/T, the fraction of the switching period for which the switch is on.
V_out = D V_in (ideal, continuous conduction).
V_out = V_in/(1 − D) (ideal, continuous conduction).
In steady state the average voltage across an inductor over one switching period is zero.
An ideal switch has zero voltage when on and zero current when off, so it dissipates no power; energy is moved by L and C.
Control that continually adjusts the PV operating voltage (via the converter's duty cycle) to the point of maximum power.
ΔI_L = (V_in − V_out) D/(f L).
A grid-connected inverter must detect loss of the grid and disconnect, protecting line workers and equipment.
Kinetic energy stored in synchronously rotating machines, released automatically to slow frequency changes after a power imbalance.
Initial RoCoF ≈ ΔP f₀/(2E_k); lower stored energy E_k means faster frequency change.
Its power electronics decouple it from grid frequency, so no rotating mass responds automatically (unless grid-forming control emulates it).
Local generation (e.g. midday PV) exceeds local demand, so power flows up the distribution network, raising voltages.
A synchronous machine running without a prime mover, providing inertia, reactive power and fault current.
Shifting or reducing flexible demand (e.g. smart EV charging) to help balance supply and demand.
An inverter controlled to set its own voltage and frequency, able to support weak grids and emulate inertia.
Energy signal: finite total energy (e.g. a pulse). Power signal: finite non-zero average power (e.g. a sinusoid, power A²/2).

cards.f: Fourier series of a square wave
cards.b: Odd harmonics only, amplitudes 4A/(nπ) for a ±A square wave: falling as 1/n.
Height A, width T ↔ AT·sin(πfT)/(πfT); first zero at f = 1/T.
Narrower pulses in time have wider spectra; bandwidth is roughly inversely proportional to duration.
Convolution in time ↔ multiplication in frequency, and vice versa.

cards.f: Effect of multiplying by cos(2πf_c t)
cards.b: Shifts the spectrum to ±f_c, each copy at half amplitude (frequency-shift/modulation property).
Gives a triangle of twice the width, peaking where the pulses fully overlap.

cards.f: Effect of a time delay on a spectrum
cards.b: Magnitude unchanged; phase gains a linear term −2πft₀.
μ = m_p/A (peak message amplitude over carrier amplitude); envelope detection needs μ ≤ 1.
2W for DSB (with or without carrier); W for single sideband.
P_total = P_c(1 + μ²/2); sideband power is P_c μ²/2.
η = μ²/(2 + μ²) for tone modulation; maximum 1/3 at μ = 1.
FM bandwidth B ≈ 2(Δf + W), where Δf is the peak deviation and W the message bandwidth.
β = Δf/W; β ≪ 1 is narrowband FM, β > 1 wideband FM.
Multiply by a synchronised local carrier cos(2πf_c t), then low-pass filter.
Information is in the frequency, not the amplitude, so a limiter can strip amplitude variations before demodulation.
A signal band-limited to B Hz can be recovered exactly if sampled at f_s ≥ 2B.
Overlap of spectral copies when f_s < 2B; high frequencies appear as low ones and cannot be removed afterwards.
R_b = n f_s (bits per sample × samples per second); telephone speech 8 × 8000 = 64 kbit/s.
About 6.02n + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine: each extra bit adds about 6 dB.
A digital repeater decides each symbol and re-creates a clean pulse, so noise does not accumulate along a link.
BPSK: two carrier phases (0, π), 1 bit/symbol. QPSK: four phases, 2 bits/symbol.
C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bit/s: the maximum error-free rate for bandwidth B with Gaussian noise.

questions.q: Silicon with n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ is doped with N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ donors. What is the equilibrium hole concentration?
questions.why: np = n_i² gives p = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ is the electron (majority) concentration, not the holes. 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ is the intrinsic value, which only applies to undoped silicon. 10⁶ cm⁻³ is N_D/n_i (10¹⁶/10¹⁰): dividing the two concentrations instead of dividing n_i² by N_D.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes p-type silicon?
options: It is doped with group V donors and its Fermi level lies closer to the valence band
It is doped with group III acceptors and its Fermi level lies closer to the conduction band
It has more holes than electrons because the band gap is smaller
It is doped with group III acceptors and its Fermi level lies closer to the valence band
questions.why: Acceptors such as boron create holes, and a high hole concentration pulls E_F towards the valence band. Group V donors produce n-type material. A Fermi level near the conduction band is the n-type picture. Doping does not change the band gap noticeably; the hole excess comes from the acceptors.

questions.q: A silicon sample is doped with N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Taking n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, μ_n = 1350 cm²/V s and q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, find the electron and hole concentrations and the resistivity. Explain why the hole contribution can be neglected.
markScheme: ρ ≈ 0.46 Ω cm, with p twelve orders of magnitude below n so its term is negligible
questions.modelAnswer: All donors are ionised at room temperature, so n ≈ N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³. From np = n_i², p = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. Conductivity σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p) ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10¹⁶ × 1350 = 2.16 S/cm, so ρ = 1/σ ≈ 0.46 Ω cm. The hole term is negligible because p is 10¹² times smaller than n while the hole mobility is of the same order as the electron mobility.

questions.q: For an ideal silicon diode at 300 K (V_T ≈ 25.9 mV) in forward bias, roughly how much extra forward voltage increases the current tenfold?
questions.why: I ∝ e^(V/V_T), so a tenfold rise needs ΔV = V_T ln 10 ≈ 59.5 mV. 26 mV is V_T itself, which multiplies the current by e ≈ 2.7, not 10. 18 mV is V_T ln 2, the step for doubling the current. 0.7 V is the typical turn-on voltage, not the step per decade of current.

questions.q: A solar cell has V_oc = 0.6 V, I_sc = 3 A and a fill factor of 0.8. What is its maximum output power?
questions.why: P_max = FF × V_oc × I_sc = 0.8 × 0.6 × 3 = 1.44 W. 1.80 W is V_oc × I_sc, which ignores the fill factor; the cell can never deliver both at once. 2.25 W divides by the fill factor instead of multiplying. 0.36 W uses (1 − FF), treating the fill factor as the fraction lost.

questions.q: A silicon solar cell has a photocurrent I_L = 3 A and saturation current I_S = 10⁻¹⁰ A, at 300 K (V_T = 25.85 mV). (a) Find V_oc. (b) The irradiance halves. Find the new I_sc and V_oc. (c) Comment on which quantity is more sensitive to light level.
markScheme: I_sc is proportional to light; V_oc only logarithmic
questions.modelAnswer: (a) V_oc = 0.025 85 × ln(3/10⁻¹⁰ + 1) = 0.025 85 × ln(3 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 0.025 85 × 24.12 ≈ 0.624 V. (b) The photocurrent is proportional to irradiance, so I_sc ≈ I_L = 1.5 A. V_oc = 0.025 85 × ln(1.5 × 10¹⁰) ≈ 0.606 V, a drop of V_T ln 2 ≈ 18 mV. (c) Current halves with the light, but voltage falls by only about 3 %, because V_oc depends on the logarithm of I_L. So a cell's output power falls roughly in proportion to irradiance, mainly through its current.

questions.q: A BJT has a common-emitter current gain β = 100. What is its common-base current gain α?
questions.why: α = β/(β + 1) = 100/101 ≈ 0.990. 0.01 is 1/β, the ratio of base to collector current. 101 is β + 1, the ratio I_E/I_B. 1.01 is (β + 1)/β = I_E/I_C, which is 1/α rather than α.

questions.q: An NMOS transistor in saturation has its overdrive voltage V_GS − V_t doubled, with V_DS still large enough for saturation. By what factor does I_D change (ignoring channel-length modulation)?
questions.why: Saturation current goes as (V_GS − V_t)², so doubling the overdrive multiplies I_D by 4. ×2 treats the dependence as linear, which is the small-V_DS triode behaviour. ×√2 would follow only if the current went as the square root of the overdrive, which inverts the square law. ×8 would need a cubic law.

questions.q: An NMOS transistor has μ_nC_ox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 10 and V_t = 0.5 V, with V_GS = 1.0 V. (a) Find the drain current in saturation and the minimum V_DS for saturation. (b) Find I_D when V_DS = 0.2 V. (c) Explain physically why the current stops increasing with V_DS in saturation.
markScheme: Overdrive 0.5 V; I_D = ½ × 2 mA/V² × 0.25 = 250 μA
Pinch-off: channel vanishes at the drain end
Extra V_DS drops across the short depleted pinch-off region, so channel voltage profile (and current) stay nearly fixed
questions.modelAnswer: (a) μ_nC_ox(W/L) = 2 mA/V² and the overdrive is 0.5 V. I_D(sat) = ½ × 2 × 0.5² = 0.25 mA = 250 μA, valid for V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_t = 0.5 V. (b) V_DS = 0.2 V is below 0.5 V, so the device is in triode: I_D = 2 mA/V² × [(0.5)(0.2) − ½(0.2)²] = 2 × 0.08 = 0.16 mA = 160 μA. (c) When V_DS reaches V_GS − V_t, the gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end falls to V_t and the inversion layer pinches off there. Further increases in V_DS are dropped across the short depleted region near the drain, so the voltage along the rest of the channel, and hence the current, stays almost constant. Electrons reaching the pinch-off point are swept to the drain by the high field.

questions.q: The same power is carried over the same line at 132 kV instead of 400 kV (unity power factor). How do the resistive line losses compare?
options: The same, because the power is the same
questions.why: Loss = P²R/V², so the ratio is (400/132)² ≈ 9.2, with the lower voltage giving the larger loss. 3.0 is the voltage ratio unsquared, forgetting that loss depends on current squared. 'Smaller' inverts the relationship, as if loss rose with voltage (V²/R thinking applied to the line). Equal power does not mean equal loss, because the current differs.

questions.q: A UK three-phase low-voltage supply has a line-to-line voltage of 400 V. What is the phase-to-neutral voltage?
questions.why: V_phase = V_line/√3 = 400/1.732 ≈ 231 V (nominally 230 V). 693 V multiplies by √3 instead of dividing. 133 V divides by 3, treating the phases as if they simply added. 400 V confuses the line voltage with the phase voltage.

questions.q: A rooftop PV panel has an area of 1.7 m² and an efficiency of 20 % at standard test conditions. (a) Find its rated power. (b) A 4 kWp system is installed at a site where the expected yield is 900 kWh per kWp per year (given). Find the annual energy and the capacity factor. (c) Give two reasons why real output is below the STC rating for much of the time.
markScheme: Reason: irradiance below 1000 W/m² (night, cloud, low sun angle, orientation)
Reason: cells hotter than 25 °C, shading, soiling or inverter losses
questions.modelAnswer: (a) At STC the irradiance is 1000 W/m², so P = 1000 × 1.7 × 0.20 = 340 W (340 Wp). (b) Annual energy = 4 kWp × 900 kWh/kWp = 3600 kWh. The maximum possible in a year is 4 kW × 8760 h = 35 040 kWh, so the capacity factor is 3600/35 040 ≈ 10.3 %. (c) Irradiance is usually well below 1000 W/m² because of night, cloud, the sun's angle and the panel's orientation and tilt. When the sun is strong, cells run much hotter than 25 °C, which lowers their voltage and power. Shading, dirt and converter losses reduce output further.

questions.q: An ideal buck converter steps 48 V down to 12 V. What duty cycle is needed?
questions.why: For a buck converter V_out = D V_in, so D = 12/48 = 0.25. 0.75 comes from the boost relation 1 − V_low/V_high, which would apply to stepping 12 V up to 48 V. 0.2 solves the buck–boost relation D/(1 − D) = 12/48. 4 is the ratio V_in/V_out turned upside down, and a duty cycle cannot exceed 1.

questions.q: Why does a grid-connected PV system use maximum power point tracking?
options: It is needed to synchronise the inverter with the grid frequency
The voltage at which the array gives most power changes with irradiance and temperature, so it must be tracked continuously
It keeps the panel at its open-circuit voltage, where output power is highest
It keeps the panel at its short-circuit current, where output power is highest
questions.why: The maximum power point moves with conditions, so the converter's duty cycle is adjusted to follow it. At open circuit the current is zero, and at short circuit the voltage is zero, so in both cases the power is zero. Grid synchronisation is a separate inverter function (usually a phase-locked loop), not the purpose of MPPT.

questions.q: An ideal buck converter has V_in = 24 V, V_out = 12 V, switching frequency 100 kHz and inductance 100 μH, and supplies a 3 A load. Find (a) the duty cycle, (b) the peak-to-peak inductor ripple current, (c) the input current, and (d) explain why the converter is far more efficient than a linear regulator doing the same job.
markScheme: Switch is fully on or off, ideally no loss; L and C transfer energy
questions.modelAnswer: (a) D = V_out/V_in = 0.5. (b) During the on-time the inductor has V_in − V_out = 12 V across it for DT = 0.5 × 10 μs = 5 μs, so ΔI_L = 12 × 5 × 10⁻⁶/(100 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.6 A peak to peak. (c) Ideal power balance: P = 12 × 3 = 36 W, so I_in = 36/24 = 1.5 A on average. (d) A linear regulator would carry the full 3 A at its input and drop 12 V across its pass transistor, wasting 36 W (50 % efficiency). The switch-mode converter's transistor is either fully on (almost no voltage) or fully off (no current), so ideally it dissipates nothing; the inductor and capacitor store and release energy to produce the lower average voltage.

questions.q: A system has 100 GW s of stored rotational kinetic energy at 50 Hz. A 1 GW generator trips. Using RoCoF ≈ ΔP f₀/(2E_k), what is the initial rate of change of frequency?
questions.why: 1 GW × 50 Hz/(2 × 100 GW s) = 0.25 Hz/s, and losing generation leaves demand exceeding supply, so the machines slow and frequency falls. 0.5 Hz/s drops the factor of 2 in the denominator. 0.005 omits f₀, giving the per-unit rate (fraction of nominal per second) rather than Hz/s. 'Rising' has the energy balance backwards: a frequency rise follows a loss of demand, not a loss of generation.

questions.q: Why can large amounts of rooftop PV cause voltage problems on a low-voltage distribution feeder at midday?
options: The feeder's resistance falls in sunlight, raising the current
Generation exceeds local demand, power flows back towards the substation and voltages along the feeder rise
PV generation lowers system frequency, which lowers voltage
PV panels draw large reactive currents at midday, causing voltage to collapse
questions.why: Feeders were designed for power flowing outwards with voltage falling along them; reverse flow makes voltage rise instead, potentially above limits. Frequency is a system-wide quantity set by the overall power balance, not a local feeder voltage effect, and extra generation would tend to raise it. PV inverters normally operate near unity power factor rather than drawing large reactive currents. Conductor resistance actually rises slightly when hot; sunlight does not reduce it.

questions.q: Explain three distinct technical challenges that electricity systems face as fossil-fuelled generation is replaced by wind and solar, and for each suggest a technical response.
markScheme: Variability/uncertainty of supply → storage, interconnectors, demand response, forecasting
Reduced inertia → faster RoCoF after faults → fast frequency response from batteries, grid-forming inverters, synchronous condensers
Distribution impacts: reverse power flow and voltage rise → active network management, tap changers, curtailment, local storage
Network capacity/location of new generation → transmission reinforcement or flexible connections
Each response linked explicitly to its mechanism, with a limitation
questions.modelAnswer: First, wind and solar output varies with weather and time of day, but supply must match demand every second. Responses include batteries and pumped hydro to shift energy, interconnectors to share surpluses, demand-side response such as smart EV charging, and better forecasting; batteries are fast but hold limited energy. Second, inverter-connected generation provides no inherent inertia, so after a large generator trips the frequency falls faster (RoCoF ≈ ΔP f₀/2E_k), risking protection trips. Responses: fast frequency response from batteries, grid-forming inverters that emulate inertia, and synchronous condensers that add rotating mass. Third, rooftop PV and new loads such as heat pumps change distribution flows; reverse power flow at midday raises feeder voltages, and evening peaks overload transformers. Responses: active network management, on-load tap changers, local storage and, as a last resort, curtailment.

questions.q: Which describes the frequency content of an ideal square wave of fundamental frequency 1 kHz with zero average value?
options: Odd harmonics only (1, 3, 5 kHz, …) with amplitudes falling as 1/n
All harmonics (1, 2, 3 kHz, …) with amplitudes falling as 1/n
Odd harmonics only with amplitudes falling as 1/n²
questions.why: The half-wave symmetry of a square wave cancels the even harmonics, and the amplitudes are 4A/(nπ). All harmonics at 1/n describes a sawtooth wave, which lacks that symmetry. Odd harmonics falling as 1/n² is a triangle wave, which has no sudden jumps. A single frequency would be a pure sinusoid; the sharp edges of a square wave need many harmonics.

questions.q: A signal passes through a linear time-invariant filter with impulse response h(t). Which statement is correct?
options: The output signal is the input multiplied by h(t)
The output spectrum is the sum of the input spectrum and the frequency response
The output spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the filter's frequency response
The output spectrum is the input spectrum convolved with the filter's frequency response
questions.why: The output is y = x * h in time, and convolution in time corresponds to multiplication in frequency: Y(f) = X(f)H(f). Convolving the spectra would correspond to multiplying the signals in time, which is modulation rather than filtering. Multiplying by h(t) in time mixes up the two operations. Adding spectra would describe two signals summed, not a filter.

questions.q: A rectangular pulse has amplitude 2 V and width 1 ms. (a) Is it an energy or a power signal? Find its energy (into 1 Ω). (b) Sketch and describe its magnitude spectrum, giving the value at f = 0 and the first zero. (c) What happens to the spectrum if the pulse width is halved?
markScheme: Value at f = 0: AT = 2 × 10⁻³ V s
First zero at 1/T = 1 kHz, sinc-shaped with decaying side lobes
Halving width: first zero moves to 2 kHz, spectrum twice as wide, peak halves
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The pulse lasts only 1 ms, so its energy is finite and its average power over all time is zero: an energy signal. E = ∫x² dt = 2² × 0.001 = 4 × 10⁻³ J (4 mJ into 1 Ω). (b) X(f) = AT·sin(πfT)/(πfT). At f = 0, X = AT = 2 × 10⁻³ V s (the area of the pulse). The magnitude has a main lobe that reaches zero at f = 1/T = 1 kHz, then decaying side lobes with zeros at every multiple of 1 kHz. (c) With T = 0.5 ms, the first zero moves to 2 kHz, so the spectrum is twice as wide, and the peak value AT halves to 1 × 10⁻³ V s. This is the time–bandwidth trade-off.

questions.q: A conventional AM transmitter is modulated by an audio signal of bandwidth 5 kHz. What bandwidth does the AM signal occupy?
options: It depends on the carrier frequency
questions.why: AM produces upper and lower sidebands each W wide, so B = 2W = 10 kHz. 5 kHz is the single-sideband bandwidth, where one sideband is removed. 20 kHz doubles twice (4W). The carrier frequency only sets where the band sits; it does not change its width.

questions.q: Broadcast FM uses a peak deviation of 75 kHz with audio bandwidth 15 kHz. What bandwidth does Carson's rule give?
questions.why: B ≈ 2(Δf + W) = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz. 150 kHz is 2Δf, leaving out the message bandwidth term. 30 kHz is 2W, the AM bandwidth, which ignores the deviation. 90 kHz is Δf + W without the factor of 2 for both sides of the carrier.

questions.q: An AM transmitter has an unmodulated carrier power of 100 W and is tone-modulated with μ = 0.5. Find (a) the total transmitted power, (b) the power in each sideband, (c) the power efficiency, and (d) explain why the efficiency is low.
markScheme: Total sideband power 12.5 W, so 6.25 W per sideband
Carrier carries no information but most of the power
Low μ makes it worse; maximum 33 % at μ = 1
questions.modelAnswer: (a) P_total = P_c(1 + μ²/2) = 100 × (1 + 0.125) = 112.5 W. (b) The sidebands together carry P_c μ²/2 = 12.5 W, split equally: 6.25 W each. (c) Efficiency = sideband power/total = 12.5/112.5 ≈ 11.1 %. (d) Only the sidebands carry the message, yet the carrier, which is present whether or not there is a message, takes 100 W. Even at μ = 1 the efficiency only reaches 1/3. The carrier is kept so that a cheap envelope detector can be used in receivers.

questions.q: A speech signal is band-limited to 4 kHz. What is the minimum sampling rate that allows perfect reconstruction?
questions.why: The Nyquist rate is 2B = 8 kHz. Sampling at 4 kHz (B itself) would make the spectral copies overlap and alias. 2 kHz halves B instead of doubling it. 16 kHz would work, but it is 4B, not the minimum.

questions.q: A signal is sampled at 8 kHz and each sample is quantised to 256 levels. What is the PCM bit rate?
questions.why: 256 levels need log₂256 = 8 bits, so R_b = 8 × 8000 = 64 kbit/s. 8 kbit/s counts one bit per sample (just the sample rate). 2.048 Mbit/s multiplies by the number of levels (256) rather than the number of bits. 32 kbit/s uses a sampling rate of 4 kHz, confusing the bandwidth with the sampling rate.

questions.q: Music band-limited to 15 kHz is sampled at 32 kHz and quantised with 8 bits per sample. (a) Is the sampling rate adequate? (b) Find the bit rate. (c) Estimate the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio for a full-scale sinusoid. (d) How many bits would be needed for at least 90 dB?
markScheme: Nyquist rate 30 kHz < 32 kHz, so adequate (with a little guard band for the anti-alias filter)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) The Nyquist rate is 2 × 15 = 30 kHz, and 32 kHz exceeds it, so aliasing is avoided provided the anti-aliasing filter cuts off sharply between 15 and 17 kHz. (b) R_b = n f_s = 8 × 32 000 = 256 kbit/s. (c) SQNR ≈ 6.02 × 8 + 1.76 ≈ 49.9 dB. (d) We need 6.02n + 1.76 ≥ 90, so n ≥ 88.24/6.02 ≈ 14.7, i.e. 15 bits; systems would normally use 16.

questions.q:
A silicon pn junction solar cell has N_A = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ on the p side and N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ on the n side. Take n_i = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and V_T = 25.85 mV.
(a) Find the minority carrier concentration on each side and the built-in potential. Sketch the equilibrium band diagram. [6]
(b) Under illumination the cell has I_L = 3 A and I_S = 10⁻¹⁰ A. Find V_oc and the current and power at V = 0.54 V (close to the maximum power point). Estimate the fill factor. [7]
(c) Sixty such cells are connected in series and operated at 0.54 V each. An ideal boost converter raises the string voltage to a 400 V DC link. Find the string power, the duty cycle and the DC-link current. [5]
(d) Explain why the converter's duty cycle must be adjusted continuously during the day. [2]
markScheme: (a) n side: p = n_i²/N_D = 10⁴ cm⁻³; p side: n = n_i²/N_A = 10³ cm⁻³
(a) V_bi = V_T ln(N_A N_D/n_i²) = 0.025 85 × ln(10¹³) ≈ 0.774 V; band diagram with flat E_F and bands bent by qV_bi
(d) MPP moves with irradiance and temperature, so MPPT must retune D
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) On the n side, electrons are the majority (n ≈ 10¹⁶ cm⁻³) and holes are p = n_i²/N_D = 10²⁰/10¹⁶ = 10⁴ cm⁻³. On the p side, p ≈ 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ and electrons are n = 10²⁰/10¹⁷ = 10³ cm⁻³. V_bi = V_T ln(N_A N_D/n_i²) = 0.025 85 × ln(10³³/10²⁰) = 0.025 85 × 29.93 ≈ 0.774 V. Band diagram: the Fermi level is flat throughout; on the p side it lies near the valence band and on the n side near the conduction band, so the bands bend down from p to n by qV_bi ≈ 0.77 eV across the depletion region (which extends mostly into the more lightly doped n side).

(b) V_oc = 0.025 85 × ln(3/10⁻¹⁰ + 1) = 0.025 85 × 24.12 ≈ 0.624 V. At 0.54 V: e^(0.54/0.025 85) = e^20.89 ≈ 1.18 × 10⁹, so the diode current is about 0.118 A and I ≈ 3 − 0.118 = 2.88 A. P = 0.54 × 2.88 ≈ 1.56 W. With I_sc ≈ 3 A, FF ≈ 1.556/(0.624 × 3) ≈ 0.83, typical of a good silicon cell (ignoring series and shunt resistance).

(c) Sixty cells in series give 60 × 0.54 = 32.4 V at 2.88 A, so P ≈ 93.4 W. For an ideal boost converter V_out = V_in/(1 − D), so D = 1 − 32.4/400 ≈ 0.919. Power is conserved, so the DC-link current is 93.4/400 ≈ 0.234 A, while the converter input current is 2.88 A.

(d) Irradiance changes I_L, and temperature changes I_S (and so V_oc), moving the maximum power point. The MPPT controller must keep adjusting D so the string stays at the voltage giving maximum power.

questions.q:
A 1 MHz carrier of amplitude 10 V is amplitude modulated by a 5 kHz tone with modulation index μ = 0.8, and the signal is delivered to a 50 Ω load.
(a) Write an expression for the AM signal and sketch its spectrum, labelling frequencies and amplitudes. [5]
(b) State the bandwidth, and find the maximum and minimum of the envelope. Can an envelope detector be used? [4]
(c) Find the carrier power, total sideband power, total power and power efficiency. [6]
(d) The same tone instead frequency modulates the carrier with a peak deviation of 25 kHz. Find the deviation ratio and estimate the bandwidth. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of FM compared with AM here. [5]
markScheme: (a) Spectrum: 10 V at 1000 kHz; 4 V at 995 kHz and 1005 kHz
(b) B = 2 × 5 = 10 kHz; envelope 18 V max, 2 V min; μ < 1 so envelope detection works
(c) Sidebands total μ²P_c/2 = 0.32 W; P_total = 1.32 W
(d) FM: better noise immunity, constant envelope; but six times the bandwidth
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) s(t) = 10[1 + 0.8 cos(2π × 5000t)] cos(2π × 10⁶t) V. Expanding with the product-to-sum identity gives 10 cos(2π × 10⁶t) + 4 cos(2π × 1.005 × 10⁶t) + 4 cos(2π × 0.995 × 10⁶t). Spectrum (positive frequencies): a carrier line of amplitude 10 V at 1000 kHz and two sideband lines of amplitude μA/2 = 4 V at 995 kHz and 1005 kHz.

(b) The signal occupies 995 to 1005 kHz, so B = 2W = 10 kHz. Envelope = 10(1 + 0.8 cos ω_m t), which varies between 10 × 1.8 = 18 V and 10 × 0.2 = 2 V. Because μ = 0.8 < 1 the envelope never goes negative and follows the message exactly, so a simple envelope detector can be used.

(c) Carrier power P_c = A²/(2R) = 100/100 = 1 W. Each sideband has amplitude 4 V, so power 16/100 = 0.16 W; the two together give 0.32 W (= μ²P_c/2 = 0.64/2 × 1). Total power 1.32 W. Efficiency = 0.32/1.32 ≈ 24.2 % (= μ²/(2 + μ²)).

(d) β = Δf/f_m = 25/5 = 5, so this is wideband FM. Carson's rule gives B ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) = 2(25 + 5) = 60 kHz. Advantage: FM has a constant envelope, so it is robust to amplitude noise and fading and allows efficient non-linear power amplifiers; with β = 5 the demodulated signal-to-noise ratio is much better. Disadvantage: it needs six times the bandwidth of AM (60 kHz against 10 kHz), and its receivers are more complex.
